newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish pound slips below parity with sterling.
newsitem.headline: Irish pound slips below parity with sterling.

text.p: The Irish pound fell below parity with sterling to its lowest level in 18 months on Friday, fuelling fears among analysts that punt/sterling weakness could stoke inflationary pressures in Ireland's booming economy.
Dealers said the move was due to sterling strength rather than punt weakness.

The Irish pound has been pulled higher against other European currencies by sterling's rise and remains perched at the top of the ERM (Exchange Rate Mechanism) grid at its highest levels against the mark for almost three years.
In late trade on Friday the punt was hovering around parity with sterling after earlier dropping to 0.9940. It was at 2.4896 marks.
Britain is Ireland's largest single trading partner and some economists warn the higher costs of British imports could spark inflation in an economy growing at the fastest rate in the EU.

Despite buoyant growth rates and strong credit growth figures, Irish inflation has remained relatively low in recent years. EU figures for September showed annualised Irish inflation running at 1.4 percent, among the lowest in the bloc.

Many economists say the punt's strength against sterling over the past year helped keep inflation low. The Irish pound broke above parity with sterling in March 1995 and climbed steadily to a high of 1.0413 sterling in August 1996.
But since then the trend has been sharply reversed. The punt fell 1.3 percent against sterling in September and 2.4 percent in October.
Dealers say the fall has been due to sterling strength combined with selling of punts by the Irish central bank.

The bank has been consitently selling punts to slow the currency's rise against the mark, due to concerns that too much volatility against the German currency could scupper Irish aspirations of joining a single currency, but this policy has attracted widespread criticism from economists.
"The central bank is taking risks with inflation similar to the UK Chancellor Nigel Lawson in 1987," said Riada Stockbrokers chief economist Dan McLaughlin.
"That triggered an inflationary boom and we could go the same way if the currency is not allowed to rise."
Some analysts, however, said the threat of inflation had been overstated.

"Imports to Ireland, it is feared, will rise in price. However, downward pressure on UK inflation and the availability of close substitutes for UK imports will inhibit any such source of inflation in Ireland," NCB Stockbrokers said.
